## Where we are

- A dated tree records the history of **lineage birth and death**. Macroevolution asks:
  what controls the **rate** of that process?
- Do **traits** — selfing, ploidy, growth form — make some lineages diversify faster?
- **Today:** the birth–death diversification model, estimating rates from trees, and
  **state-dependent diversification** (BiSSE/HiSSE) with its pitfalls.

## Learning objectives

By the end you should be able to:

- Define **speciation $\lambda$, extinction $\mu$**, net diversification $r$, and turnover.
- Read a **lineage-through-time (LTT)** plot.
- Explain the **BiSSE** model and what it estimates.
- Explain why naive SSE tests give **false positives**, and how **HiSSE**/CID nulls respond.

# Diversification as a birth–death process {.center}

## Speciation, extinction, and net rate

Model a clade as a **birth–death process**: lineages speciate at rate $\lambda$ and go
extinct at rate $\mu$.

$$
\text{net diversification } r = \lambda - \mu, \qquad
\text{turnover } \epsilon = \frac{\mu}{\lambda}.
$$

- The **same** process was the tree prior for dating (phylo deck 02) — here it is the
  **object of inference**.
- Extinction is estimable from **extant-only** trees (via the shape of the branching
  times), though it is the hardest parameter to pin down.

## Lineage-through-time (LTT) plots

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="55%"}
- Plot $\log(\text{number of lineages})$ vs. time.
- **Constant-rate** pure birth ⟹ straight line (slope $= r$).
- **Slowdowns** (concave) suggest diversity-dependence or declining rates; **upturns**
  suggest recent radiation (or the "pull of the present" from extinction).
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.figure-prompt}
**FIGURE** — LTT plot: a constant-rate line vs. a decelerating (concave) curve, log-scale
y-axis against time.

## Rate variation across the tree

- Rates need not be constant: **episodic** birth–death and methods like **BAMM** allow
  rate shifts along branches (conceptual here).
- The question that follows: are rate shifts associated with **traits**?

# State-dependent diversification {.center}

## BiSSE — does a trait drive diversification?

**BiSSE** couples a binary trait's evolution to the birth–death rates [@maddison2007]:

$$
\lambda_0,\ \lambda_1 \quad(\text{speciation in state 0/1}),\qquad
\mu_0,\ \mu_1 \quad(\text{extinction}),
$$
$$
q_{01},\ q_{10}\quad(\text{trait transition rates}).
$$

- Jointly models trait changes **and** diversification along the tree.
- Asks: is $\lambda_1 \neq \lambda_0$ (does the trait affect speciation)?
- Extensions: **MuSSE** (multistate), **QuaSSE** (continuous), **ChromoSSE**
  (chromosome number — polyploidy!), **GeoSSE** (geography — biogeography lecture).

## The false-positive problem

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="56%"}
- BiSSE has a serious flaw: **any** neutral trait that happens to correlate with a
  diversification shift somewhere on the tree can look "significant" [@rabosky2015].
- A single radiating clade that also happens to share a trait state fools the test.
- ⟹ naive BiSSE **rejects the null too often**.
:::

::: {.column width="44%"}
::: {.figure-prompt}
**FIGURE** — cartoon: one fast-diversifying clade carrying trait state 1 tricks BiSSE into
inferring the trait "causes" speciation, though the shift is elsewhere.
:::

## HiSSE and the CID null

- **HiSSE** (Hidden-State SSE) adds an **unobserved** trait so that diversification shifts
  can be driven by something *other* than the focal trait [@beaulieu2016].
- Compare against a **character-independent diversification (CID)** null — a HiSSE model
  where rate shifts exist but are **decoupled** from the observed trait.
- If HiSSE/CID fits as well, the focal trait is **not** the driver.

::: {.callout-important}
The lesson: SSE models test *association*, and association is easily spurious on a single
tree. Always fit a **hidden-state / trait-independent null** before claiming a trait drives
diversification. <span class="xref">→ the diversification practical does exactly this.</span>
:::

# Plants {.center}

## Trait-dependent diversification in plants

- **Selfing** (popgen deck 03): often a "dead-end" — higher extinction / lower net
  diversification over macroevolutionary time.
- **Polyploidy** (popgen deck 06): WGD's effect on diversification is debated —
  **ChromoSSE** models chromosome-number change and diversification jointly.
- **Growth form, pollination syndrome, breeding system, range** — all classic SSE
  questions in plants.

::: {.callout-tip}
These traits recur across the course: what raises or lowers a plant lineage's **birth and
death rates** over millions of years?
:::

## Summary

- Diversification = a **birth–death** process; $r=\lambda-\mu$, read partly from **LTT**
  plots.
- **BiSSE** couples a trait to $\lambda,\mu$ — but is prone to **false positives**.
- **HiSSE + CID nulls** guard against attributing shifts to the wrong (or a neutral) trait.
- In plants, selfing and polyploidy are the headline trait-diversification questions.
- <span class="xref">→ practical: fit BiSSE then HiSSE in RevBayes and compare.</span>
